summary: This informational memo introduces the Internet to arts and humanities communities, describing it as a tool and medium for creating, presenting and preserving arts and humanities content. It is a guide for newcomers.

eli5.summary: A friendly beginner's tour of the Internet for artists and writers.

questions: what is the world wide web
subtitle: A guide to the Internet for artists, writers, and humanities scholars.

tldr.problem: Artists and humanities scholars are underrepresented on the Internet, and many lack knowledge of how the Internet can be used as a tool for collaboration, distribution, and presentation of their work.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a comprehensive introduction to Internet concepts, tools, and platforms (web, email, newsgroups, chat) with practical guidance on creating and sharing arts and humanities content online.
tldr.outcome: Artists and scholars gain practical knowledge to establish an online presence, collaborate globally, and participate in the emerging digital culture.

today: RFC 2150 is Informational and remains a good historical snapshot of how the Internet was understood by non-technical communities in 1997. The technical foundations it describes (IP, TCP, HTTP, HTML) remain unchanged; what has changed dramatically is the ubiquity of broadband, the shift from static web pages to interactive platforms, and the rise of social media and streaming services. Nevertheless, its core message about the importance of arts and humanities on the Internet remains relevant.

sections.title: Arts and Humanities on the Internet
sections.content:
The RFC argues that as the Internet grows in cultural importance, the Arts and Humanities communities must actively participate to ensure human culture is well-represented online. The Internet began as a technical network built by scientists and engineers, but is becoming a medium for education, entertainment, and cultural exchange. Artists are needed to bring heart and soul to what would otherwise be a purely technical infrastructure.

The RFC defines Arts broadly, including dance, design, visual arts, music, theater, and literary arts. Humanities encompasses language, literature, history, philosophy, archaeology, religion, and cultural studies. The authors use Artist to mean anyone engaged in creating, studying, curating, or presenting cultural works.
sections.eli5: The Internet started as a tool for scientists, but now it can show art, music, books, and history to people all over the world. Artists should help make the Internet a place where human creativity shines.

sections.title: What the Internet Is and How It Works
sections.content:
The Internet is people, computers, and information electronically linked by common communication protocols. It evolved from the ARPANET, a network created by the Advanced Research Projects Agency in the 1960s. As other networks connected to it, the interconnected system became the Internet.

The Internet is built on two core protocols: IP (Internet Protocol), which routes packets of data between computers using addresses, and TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), which guarantees reliable delivery by having the receiver acknowledge data. These form the TCP/IP suite that is the heart of the Internet. Other higher-level protocols include HTTP (web), SMTP (email), FTP (file transfer), NNTP (news), and Telnet (remote login).

Every computer on the Internet has a unique IP address (four numbers separated by dots) and a human-readable hostname (like www.example.com). Information on the web is located using URLs (like http://www.example.com/page.html), which specify the protocol, hostname, and file path.
sections.eli5: The Internet is a huge network of computers connected by special rules called protocols. Every computer and website has an address, just like a house. When you type a web address, your computer talks to another computer to get the information you want.

sections.title: The World Wide Web and Hypertext
sections.content:
The World Wide Web is a subset of the Internet consisting of pages written in HTML (HyperText Markup Language) that are stored on web servers and retrieved using HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) by web browsers.

HTML is a simple markup format that lets creators specify fonts, links, images, and layout within a text file. The key innovation is hypertext: clickable links that connect words or pictures to other pages. Unlike traditional linear text, hypertext lets readers follow many different paths through interconnected ideas, much more naturally resembling how human thought works.

A web site consists of pages stored on one or more servers, starting with a home page that links to other related pages. Each page is a file with its own URL. The RFC notes that there are already hundreds of thousands of web sites, ranging from personal pages (family photos, hobbies) to business sites, to cultural institutions.
sections.eli5: The web is like a giant encyclopedia where you can click on highlighted words to jump to related pages. Authors can link their pages to each other, so readers can explore in any order they want, following what interests them.

sections.title: Communication and Community Forums
sections.content:
The Internet provides multiple forums for artists to communicate and collaborate. Message-based forums (email, newsgroups, bulletin boards) let users send messages that others read and respond to later. Real-time forums (chat, IRC, audio/video conferencing) let multiple people interact simultaneously. Games and virtual worlds (MUDs, Multi-User Dungeons) allow collaborative and creative play.

Email is the most accessible and personal form of communication, using addresses like username@hostname.com. Newsgroups allow group discussions organized by topic, retrieved using NNTP (Network News Transfer Protocol). Artists use these forums to share work, get feedback, collaborate on projects, and find peers with similar interests.
sections.eli5: Artists can send messages to each other (email), join group discussions (newsgroups), or chat live with people interested in the same art forms. Some places let multiple people work together on creative projects over the Internet.

sections.title: Creating and Sharing Arts Content Online
sections.content:
Artists can share many types of content online: text (poetry, stories, transcripts), images (paintings, photographs, sculptures), sound (music, readings, audio art), video (performance, video art), and descriptions of their process and work. The RFC describes file formats for each medium: text formats (HTML, plain text), image formats (bitmap like GIF and JPEG, vector like EPS), video formats, and audio formats.

To put work on the Internet, artists typically: choose a file format suitable for their medium; learn basic tools (HTML editors, graphics software, audio software); find or build a web site; write descriptions and links; and publicize their work. The RFC emphasizes that many tools are freely available via the Internet itself (shareware, public domain, and open-source software).

Creating an online presence allows artists to reach a global audience, collaborate with peers worldwide, get feedback from critics and enthusiasts, and establish visibility for their work.
sections.eli5: Artists can put pictures, music, writing, and video online for the whole world to see. Tools to create and share this work are often free or cheap. You can reach audiences far away and get feedback from people interested in your art.

sections.title: Security, Copyright, and Practical Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several challenges for online arts and humanities work. Security is important: artists should talk to their ISP about security policies, keep software up-to-date, and use available security tools. Viruses can be transmitted through downloads, so use antivirus software and be cautious with executable files.

Copyright and intellectual property are significant concerns. Artists need to understand their own rights to their work and respect the rights of others. The RFC advises seeking professional legal advice on copyright, trademark, and privacy issues. Netiquette (network etiquette) is important in forums: follow community norms, be respectful, and avoid harassment.

The RFC concludes that the Internet represents the new frontier for human growth and creativity. The day is coming when artists not on the Internet will be greatly handicapped in expressing and distributing their work. For artists and scholars, engaging with the Internet is becoming essential.
sections.eli5: When sharing your work online, be careful about who you give personal information to, protect your copyright so nobody steals your ideas, and be polite when talking to people in online communities.
